_comment: Career Explorer configuration — deterministic, reviewable. Families map SOC major groups (2 digits), minor groups (4 chars '15-1'), 6-digit codes, or full O*NET-SOC codes to student-friendly families; a career may belong to several families. `familiar` lists well-known 6-digit codes excluded from the 'careers you may not know exist' collection. `subjects` map school subjects to O*NET Knowledge elements (importance 1–5). `traits` map 'what you like doing' to O*NET work activities (wa, importance 1–5), work context (cx, 1–5), interests (ri, RIASEC 1–7) and knowledge (kn, 1–5): a career carries the trait when ANY component meets its minimum. No model is involved in any mapping.

families.label: Health and human care
families.blurb: Caring for people's bodies and minds — from emergency rooms to therapy offices to labs that read your blood test.

families.label: Technology and computing
families.blurb: Building, securing and running the software, networks and data systems everything else depends on.

families.label: Science and research
families.blurb: Asking how the world works — in labs, in the field, with data — and publishing what you find.

families.label: Design and creativity
families.blurb: Making things people see, hear, wear, play and live in — from buildings and games to stage and screen.

families.label: Business and entrepreneurship
families.blurb: Running organizations, selling, budgeting, analyzing markets and starting things.

families.label: Law and public policy
families.blurb: Rules, rights and how society decides things — courts, legislatures, agencies and the people who navigate them.

families.label: Education
families.blurb: Helping people learn — in classrooms, libraries, museums, gyms and online.

families.label: Skilled trades
families.blurb: Building, installing, fixing and making real things with your hands and your head.

families.label: Engineering and infrastructure
families.blurb: Designing and keeping up the systems a modern place runs on — bridges, power, water, machines, chips.

families.label: Environment and sustainability
families.blurb: Land, water, energy, climate and the living things that depend on them.

families.label: Media and communication
families.blurb: Telling stories and getting messages across — writing, video, audio, marketing, news.

families.label: Community and social services
families.blurb: Standing with people through hard times — counseling, social work, faith, child and family support.

families.label: Transportation and logistics
families.blurb: Moving people and things — planes, ships, trains, trucks, warehouses and the planning behind them.

families.label: Hospitality and experiences
families.blurb: Food, travel, events, sport, wellness — creating experiences people remember.

families.label: Public safety
families.blurb: Protecting people, places and systems — emergency response, law enforcement, security, inspection.

families.label: Emerging and interdisciplinary careers
families.blurb: Roles that sit between fields or barely existed a decade ago — many have no official category yet.

creativity.label: Creating things
creativity.blurb: Work where coming up with original ideas, designs or performances is a big part of the job.

technology.label: Working with technology
technology.blurb: Computers, software, electronics or automated systems are central to the daily work.

helping.label: Helping people directly
helping.blurb: Caring for, teaching, counseling or personally assisting people is at the heart of the work.

outdoors.label: Working outdoors
outdoors.blurb: A large share of the work happens outside, in all kinds of weather.
any_of: Outdoors, Exposed to All Weather Conditions

building.label: Building and fixing things
building.blurb: Hands-on work with tools, materials, machines or structures.

analysis.label: Analyzing and figuring things out
analysis.blurb: Investigating, working with data and solving hard problems is the core of the job.

communication.label: Communicating and persuading
communication.blurb: Explaining, presenting, writing, performing or persuading people is a big part of the work.
any_of: Communicating with People Outside the Organization
Performing for or Working Directly with the Public

test_ideas._comment: Generic, deterministic ways to test a career before committing — chosen by Job Zone and family. Labelled as general suggestions, not personalized advice.
always: Find two people who do this job (a family friend, a teacher's contact, a local employer) and ask them what a normal week actually looks like — and what they would tell a student considering it.
Read three current job postings for this title and list the tools, tasks and qualifications they repeat. Compare them with the task list on this page.
After a week of small experiments, write down honestly which parts felt energizing and which felt like a chore — that is the real signal.
zone_1_2: Try a short shift, volunteer slot or summer job in this kind of setting — most of these roles can be sampled in weeks, not years.
zone_3: Look up a local community-college or apprenticeship program for this field and sit in on an intro session or open house.
zone_4_5: Take (or audit) an introductory class in the main knowledge area listed above and notice whether the hard parts feel worth it.
Ask someone in the field how they spent their first two years after school — the entry path is often different from the job title.

health: Volunteer in a clinic, hospital, pharmacy or care home to see whether being around patients energizes or drains you.
tech: Build one small project end to end (a website, a script, a game level) and see whether debugging it is satisfying or infuriating.
science: Join a science fair, citizen-science project or a lab open day; keep a notebook of questions you actually wanted answered.
design: Make a small portfolio piece for a real 'client' (a club poster, a friend's logo, a room plan) and take feedback on it.
business: Run something tiny with a budget — a bake sale, a resale side-hustle, a club event — and track what you spent and earned.
law: Attend a public court session or a city-council meeting; note what the professionals in the room actually did.
education: Tutor a younger student for a month; notice whether explaining things repeatedly is rewarding to you.
trades: Take a hands-on class (wood, metal, electrical, auto) or shadow a tradesperson for a day; try a real repair at home.
engineering: Join a robotics, bridge-building or maker club, or take apart and reassemble something mechanical.
environment: Volunteer with a park, watershed or conservation group and see whether outdoor fieldwork suits you.
media: Produce one piece for a real audience — a short video, a podcast episode, a school newspaper story — and watch how people respond.
community: Volunteer at a food bank, shelter or youth program; notice how you feel after a day of it.
transport: Ask for a ride-along or a warehouse or airport tour; look at how the planning behind the moving actually happens.
hospitality: Work a few shifts in food service or events; pay attention to whether a busy room gives you energy.
safety: Go to a fire-station or police open house, take a first-aid or CPR class, and ask about ride-alongs or explorer programs.
emerging: Search for the role's professional community online and read what people actually do all day; try one free introductory course in the field.
